To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the following upper bounds are derived: (a) for all superparticles (except the gravitino) and for the lightest Higgs boson: m ≤ 1.2 TeV, where m is the top quark pole mass (b) for the lightest neutralino: m ≤ 0.5 TeV (c) for the light Higgs boson, m h ≤ 130 GeV, where m h is the pole mass (d) for the gluino
(a) the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) must be a neutralino, (b) the LSP must be lighter than about 100–200 GeV, and (c) squarks and gluinos can become as heavy as 1 TeV or so

(i) the mass of the lightest superparticle (LSP) is bounded from above by the top quark (TQ) mass, and (ii) the masses of strongly-interacting superparticles are bounded by the TQ mass squared divided by 8π, i.e., by 100 GeV or 1 TeV, depending on the TQ mass.

the study of supersymmetric models, and in particular with the search for the lightest Higgs boson in the minimal supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model (MSSM).

the naturalness criterion, in its most general form, implies the existence of a light chargino or neutralino, with a mass below 100–200 GeV, but it is compatible with gluinos and squarks heavier than 1 TeV, and with a top quark mass as large as 200 GeV.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the top quark is the only superparticle that is not constrained by naturalness.
the superparticle mass bounds are very sensitive to the top quark, and that the top quark is a crucial ingredient in any attempt to test supersymmetry at future accelerators.

, if supersymmetry is a good candidate for physics beyond the Standard Model, the superparticle mass spectrum must be strongly hierarchical, with weakly interacting super-particles lighter than 100 GeV, and strongly interacting superparticles heavier than 500 GeV.
